plan.angle: Keep the calm myth correction, with these changes. (1) BMJ cohort, adults with type 2 diabetes only: 1.37 times the risk vs SGLT-2 inhibitors and 1.68 times vs DPP-4 inhibitors. Label these as relative risks, say the authors call the absolute risk low, and say the hair loss was nonscarring, so it may be reversible. (2) NYU: describe it as 'a genetic study, not a study of people taking the drugs, suggested a small (~7%) added risk of male-pattern hair loss in men already genetically predisposed.' (3) Explain telogen effluvium and that it is typically temporary. (4) Levers, strongest first: enough protein, a weight-loss pace agreed with your prescriber, and asking your doctor about checking ferritin/iron, vitamin D and thyroid. (5) See a dermatologist if shedding lasts more than about 6 months, comes in patches, or is scarring or painful. No supplement promises, and don't stop the medicine without your prescriber. Title: 'Ozempic Hair Loss: How Common It Really Is and Why It Often Grows Back'. Cite the review by its exact title (e.g. American Journal of Clinical Dermatology 2026).

plan.why: Highest momentum on the radar (82), with heavy search demand. The Guardian and Times of India explainers ran Sep 27–28. An evergreen side-effect question with a fresh hook, in the 'getting the most from GLP-1' pillar. | fact-check: BMJ study, confirmed via bmjgroup.com and Healio. Adults with type 2 diabetes starting a GLP-1 were compared with adults starting other diabetes drugs, using Penn Medicine electronic health records. Nonscarring alopecia risk was 1.37 times higher than with SGLT-2 inhibitors (12,004 vs 15,221 people) and 1.68 times higher than with DPP-4 inhibitors (11,964 vs 11,238). These are relative risks, and the authors say the absolute risk is low. The NYU Langone study (Journal of Investigative Dermatology, published September 3, 2026) is a genetic study. It used variation in the GLP1R gene as a stand-in for drug activity in more than 205,000 men, and it did not observe people actually taking GLP-1 drugs. It found about 7% added risk of androgenetic alopecia in men who are predisposed, which the script must describe as genetic evidence. Saying 'GLP-1 use may speed up hair loss' as if patients were studied would overstate it. The 'Clinical Dermatology review Sep 2026' could not be identified as named. Candidates that do exist are 'The Impact of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists on Hair' in the American Journal of Clinical Dermatology (2026, PubMed 41957308) and Gupta et al.'s 2026 systematic review (PMC13100445). Cite one of these by its exact title. In the title, soften 'usually grows back' to 'often grows back'. The telogen effluvium evidence supports 'typically temporary', not a guarantee.

package.description:
Ozempic and GLP-1 hair loss: how common is it, really? Here's what a 2026 study of adults with type 2 diabetes, a genetic study from NYU Langone, and a new dermatology review show, plus why hair often grows back.

Quick answer: In semaglutide (Wegovy) trials, about 3% of people reported hair loss vs 1% on placebo. A 2026 observational study of adults with type 2 diabetes (publicized by BMJ Group) found about 1.37 times the relative risk of a hair loss diagnosis on GLP-1 medicines vs SGLT-2 inhibitors (roughly 7 vs 5 cases per 1,000 people per year), and about 1.68 times vs DPP-4 inhibitors. These were two separate comparisons. It shows a link, not proof that the drug causes hair loss, and it may not apply to people using these medicines for weight. The extra risk was in nonscarring hair loss, where follicles stay intact, so regrowth is possible. The study couldn't check how severe it was or whether hair grew back. The pattern most often described is telogen effluvium: delayed, even shedding that's typically temporary. A 2026 review points to rapid weight loss, and possibly lower food and nutrient intake, as likely contributors, though the exact mechanism isn't settled.

This video is for general education only and isn't medical advice. GLP-1 medicines are prescription drugs. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether one is right for you, and don't stop or change your medication on your own.

Sources:
1. GLP-1 diabetes drugs linked to increased risk of hair loss (BMJ Group, 2026): https://bmjgroup.com/glp-1-diabetes-drugs-linked-to-increased-risk-of-hair-loss/
2. A causal effect of increased GLP1R expression on Male Pattern Hair Loss is suggested by Two-Sample Mendelian Randomization (Journal of Investigative Dermatology, 2026): https://www.jidonline.org/article/S0022-202X(26)02729-6/abstract
3. The Impact of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists on Hair: Beneficial Effects or Adverse Outcomes? (American Journal of Clinical Dermatology, 2026): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41957308/
4. Do you have hair loss or hair shedding? (American Academy of Dermatology): https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/insider/shedding
5. WEGOVY (semaglutide) Prescribing Information (FDA, 2021): https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2021/215256s000lbl.pdf
6. Telogen Effluvium (StatPearls, 2024): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430848/
7. Nutritional priorities to support GLP-1 therapy for obesity: a joint Advisory (Am J Clin Nutr, 2025): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40445127/
8. Diet and hair loss: effects of nutrient deficiency and supplement use (Dermatol Pract Concept, 2017): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28243487/
9. Biotin Interference with Troponin Lab Tests (FDA, 2019): https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/in-vitro-diagnostics/biotin-interference-troponin-lab-tests-assays-subject-biotin-interference
10. Hair loss types: CCCA signs and symptoms (American Academy of Dermatology): https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/hair-loss/types/ccca/symptoms

What you'll learn:
• Why hair sheds months after starting a GLP-1, not right away
• What telogen effluvium is and why it's typically temporary
• What the new diabetes cohort study really shows (relative vs absolute risk)
• What a genetic (Mendelian randomization) study can and can't tell you about male-pattern hair loss
• Three levers: protein first, a weight-loss pace agreed with your prescriber, and labs worth asking your doctor about (ferritin, vitamin D, thyroid)
• Three warning signs that mean it's time to see a dermatologist

script.working_title: Ozempic Hair Loss: How Common It Really Is and Why It Often Grows Back
script.hook_pattern: Counterintuitive claim + open loop (the clue is on your calendar, not in your medicine cabinet; three warning signs and a supplement that can throw off blood tests, paid off at the end)

scenes.narration: More hair in your brush, a few months into a GLP-1. It's easy to assume the medicine is attacking your hair. But the most important clue might be on your calendar, not in your medicine cabinet.

visual.stock_query: worried person holding hairbrush, wall calendar

scenes.retention_device: Counterintuitive claim that opens the main loop (why timing matters)

scenes.narration: A big new study found that hair loss was more common in adults with type two diabetes who started a GLP-1 than in those starting some other diabetes drugs. The headlines ran with it.

But the researchers themselves call the absolute risk low. And the extra risk showed up in nonscarring hair loss, the kind where follicles stay intact, so regrowth is possible. The study couldn't check how severe it was or whether hair grew back.

visual.myth: The headlines: GLP-1s cause hair loss
visual.fact: Authors: absolute risk low; extra risk was nonscarring type

scenes.retention_device: But/therefore reversal of the headline, with the study's key limitation

scenes.narration: In the next few minutes, you'll learn how common this really is, why it happens, and which three steps have the strongest reasoning behind them for protecting your hair.

And stay to the end. There are three warning signs that mean your shedding is probably not the usual temporary kind, plus one hugely popular hair supplement that can quietly throw off your blood tests.

visual.stock_query: supplement bottle beside blood test tube

scenes.retention_device: Open loop paid off in the supplement and warning-sign chapters

scenes.narration: Let's start with the simplest question. How often does this actually happen?

visual.stock_query: chapter card question mark hair strand

scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset with a direct question

scenes.narration: In the trials behind Wegovy's approval, the weight-management version of semaglutide, hair loss was reported by about three out of every hundred adults.

visual.stat_label: Adults reporting hair loss, semaglutide trials

scenes.narration: On placebo, it was about one in a hundred. So it's real, it's more common than on a dummy injection, and the large majority of people didn't report it.

visual.stock_query: two small bar charts side by side

scenes.narration: Here's the twist. Some shedding is completely normal. Dermatologists say losing about fifty to one hundred hairs a day is typical.

visual.stat_label: Hairs shed per day, typically normal

scenes.narration: So the real question isn't 'am I losing hair?' Everyone is. It's 'am I losing noticeably more than my normal?'
And when you do notice more, the first suspect is usually the drug. But this summer's headline study is more nuanced than it looks.
Here's how to read that study without panicking.
Researchers used electronic health records from Penn Medicine. They followed adults with type two diabetes who were starting a new diabetes medicine.
Then they compared people starting a GLP-1 with people starting two other common drug classes: SGLT two inhibitors and DPP four inhibitors.

The first comparison was about twelve thousand people on a GLP-1 versus about fifteen thousand on an SGLT two inhibitor. The second was about twelve thousand on a GLP-1 versus about eleven thousand on a DPP four inhibitor.

visual.stock_query: two crowds of cartoon people facing off

scenes.narration: Compared with SGLT two inhibitors, GLP-1 users had about one point three seven times the risk of being diagnosed with hair loss. In real numbers, that's roughly seven versus five cases per thousand people followed for a year.

visual.stat_label: Hazard ratio vs SGLT-2 (≈7 vs 5 per 1,000 per year)

scenes.retention_device: Headline stat reveal, with absolute numbers alongside

scenes.narration: Compared with DPP four inhibitors, it was about one point six eight times the risk of any hair loss diagnosis.
Those multipliers sound dramatic. But they're relative risks. They tell you how much higher the risk was than in another group, not how many people actually lost hair.

visual.myth: 1.37× means lots of people lose hair
visual.fact: It's a relative risk vs another group

scenes.narration: And the authors describe the absolute risk as low. Think of it this way: a bigger slice of a small pie is still a small slice.

visual.stock_query: tiny pie with slightly bigger slice

scenes.narration: One more subtlety. These were two separate comparisons, with different people in each. So one point six eight isn't a scarier version of one point three seven. They're answers to two different questions.

visual.stock_query: two different rulers side by side

scenes.narration: It was also observational, and the authors say other unmeasured factors can't be ruled out. It shows a link, not proof that the drug itself harms hair. And it only included adults with type two diabetes, so it may not apply to everyone using these medicines for weight.

items: Other factors can't be ruled out
May not apply to weight use
visual.stock_query: chain link icon with question mark

scenes.retention_device: Limitations stated plainly to build trust

scenes.narration: Now, remember the word that matters most in that paper: nonscarring. Hold on to it, because it's the key to why hair often grows back.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop, paid off in the hair clock chapter

scenes.narration: But first, the other headline you might have seen. The one about men and male-pattern baldness.

visual.stock_query: man looking at receding hairline mirror

scenes.narration: Researchers at NYU Langone published a study in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology on September third.
Here's the surprising part. They didn't study people taking GLP-1 drugs at all. They looked at natural variation in the GLP-1 receptor gene in more than two hundred and five thousand men.

visual.stat_label: Men studied through genes, not drug use
visual.stock_query: crowd of men with DNA strands

scenes.retention_device: But here's where it gets weird: surprising design

scenes.narration: Some people are born with gene versions that make more of the GLP-1 receptor, the same switch these drugs press. Scientists use that as a stand-in, a kind of natural experiment that starts at birth.
This genetic study, not a study of people taking the drugs, suggested about seven percent higher odds of male-pattern hair loss in men already genetically predisposed to it.

visual.stat_label: Higher relative odds, genetic estimate, predisposed men only

scenes.narration: And those are relative odds, estimated from genes rather than measured in patients. It's an interesting clue for researchers, not a verdict on your hairline.

visual.myth: GLP-1s speed up baldness in men
visual.fact: Genetic clue only; patients weren't studied

scenes.narration: So neither study says GLP-1s make people go bald. Which leads to the real question. If hair does shed, why? This is where it gets interesting.
Every hair on your head runs on its own clock.
At any moment, most of your hairs are in a growing phase that can last years. A smaller share are in a resting phase, getting ready to fall out and make room.

items: Growing phase: most hairs, lasts years
Resting phase: smaller share, then sheds

scenes.narration: When your body goes through a big physical stress, lots of growing hairs can get pushed into that resting phase at the same time.

visual.stock_query: many follicles switching to sleep mode

scenes.narration: Then, roughly two to three months later, they let go together. Doctors call this telogen effluvium.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the calendar clue begins

scenes.narration: Known triggers include a high fever, surgery, giving birth, a major illness, and losing a lot of weight.
In fact, the American Academy of Dermatology lists losing twenty pounds or more as one of the common triggers of excessive shedding.

visual.stat_label: Weight loss listed as shedding trigger

scenes.narration: Now, remember the calendar clue from the very start? Shedding that begins a few months after weight starts coming off quickly fits this pattern.
That's why a twenty twenty-six review on GLP-1s and hair points to rapid weight loss, and possibly lower food and nutrient intake, as likely contributors. The exact mechanism still isn't settled.

visual.stock_query: research review on desk, question mark

scenes.narration: Here's the payoff of that word, nonscarring. In telogen effluvium, the follicles aren't destroyed. They're resting.
That's why this kind of shedding is typically temporary. Once the trigger settles, follicles can restart the growing phase.
According to dermatologists, hair usually regains its normal fullness within about six to nine months. That's a common path, not a guarantee.

visual.stat_label: Usual time to regain normal fullness

scenes.narration: There's a catch. Regrowth is slow, and new hairs start out short. So your hair can still look thin for a while, even while it's recovering.

visual.stock_query: short new hairs sprouting on scalp

scenes.narration: So what can you actually do? Three levers, starting with the one that has the strongest support.

visual.stock_query: three big levers on control panel

scenes.narration: Protein. Pace. And checking for hidden gaps.
Hair is built mainly from a protein called keratin. And when your appetite drops on a GLP-1, it's easy to fall short on protein without noticing.

visual.stock_query: hair strand made of protein blocks

scenes.narration: A joint advisory from four major nutrition and obesity medicine groups says protein should be a priority for people on GLP-1 therapy, mainly to help protect muscle. The same habit also covers a building block your hair needs.
scenes.on_screen_text: Experts: prioritize protein to help protect muscle

visual.stat_label: Joint advisory: ACLM, ASN, OMA, TOS (2025)

scenes.narration: The practical version: eat your protein first at each meal. Eggs, Greek yogurt, fish, chicken, tofu, beans or lentils. A dietitian can help you find the amount that fits you.
Lever two is pace. Big, fast drops in weight are exactly the kind of stress linked to shedding.
But you don't set that pace alone. It's something to agree on with your prescriber, who manages your treatment plan and can adjust it if needed.
scenes.on_screen_text: Set the pace with your prescriber

scenes.narration: Lever three: look for hidden gaps. Low iron stores, low vitamin D and thyroid problems have all been linked to hair loss, and nutrient gaps are something experts say to watch for during GLP-1 treatment.
So it's reasonable to ask your doctor whether checking ferritin, which reflects your iron stores, along with vitamin D and thyroid function, makes sense for you.
Finding and treating a real deficiency is very different from taking pills just in case. Which brings us to the supplement aisle.
scenes.on_screen_text: Real gap vs just in case
scenes.retention_device: Transition teaser toward promised supplement payoff

scenes.narration: Hair gummies. Biotin. Hair, skin and nails blends. They're everywhere.
A review of diet and hair loss found little evidence that these supplements help people who aren't actually deficient.

visual.myth: Hair gummies regrow hair for everyone
visual.fact: Little evidence if you're not deficient

scenes.narration: And more isn't always better. That same review notes that too much of some nutrients, including vitamin A and selenium, is itself linked to hair loss.
Now, the supplement I promised at the start. The FDA has warned that biotin, a very popular hair supplement, can interfere with some lab tests and cause falsely high or falsely low results.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the supplement open loop

scenes.narration: One test the FDA highlighted is troponin, which doctors use to help diagnose heart attacks. A falsely low result there could lead to a missed diagnosis.
So if you take biotin or any supplement, tell your doctor before blood work. FDA notes it can affect some thyroid and ferritin tests too, the very checks we just talked about.

visual.stock_query: patient handing supplement list to nurse

scenes.retention_device: Solution after stakes, callback to the lab checks

scenes.narration: The bottom line: supplements aren't a shortcut. Fix real gaps with your doctor, and let food do the everyday work.

visual.fact: Fix real deficiencies; food does daily work

scenes.narration: Now, the three warning signs I promised.

visual.stock_query: three warning flags on scalp map

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the second opening loop

scenes.narration: Sign one: time. If heavy shedding lasts more than about six months, see a dermatologist. Shedding that drags on that long is considered chronic, and it deserves a closer look.

visual.stat_label: Shedding this long: see a dermatologist

scenes.narration: Sign two: patches. Telogen effluvium usually thins hair evenly all over the scalp. Round bald patches, or one area thinning much faster than the rest, point to something else.

Sign three: scalp changes. If the skin where hair has gone looks scaly, bumpy or shiny, especially with burning, itching or pain, that can be a sign of scarring hair loss, which dermatologists want to see early.
Whatever you notice, don't stop or change your medication on your own. Bring it to your prescriber. There are often things to adjust around the medicine first.
So let's put it all together.
Hair loss on a GLP-1 is real, but in the trials it affected a small minority, and the new study's authors call the absolute risk low.

visual.stat_label: Reported hair loss: semaglutide vs placebo trials

scenes.narration: The pattern most often described is telogen effluvium, a delayed, even shedding after fast weight loss. It's typically temporary, and hair often grows back.

Your checklist. Put protein first at every meal. Agree on a sensible pace with your prescriber. Ask about ferritin, vitamin D and thyroid. Skip megadose supplements. And see a dermatologist for any of the three warning signs.

visual.stock_query: checklist with hair and plate icons

scenes.narration: Then give it time. Your follicles are on a slow clock, and patience is part of the plan.
scenes.on_screen_text: Patience is part of the plan
scenes.retention_device: Emotional close, callback to hair clock

scenes.narration: If you're wondering whether a GLP-1 medicine is right for you, or a side effect is worrying you, talk to your doctor or prescriber.

Hair isn't the only thing that needs protein on a GLP-1. Your muscle does too. Subscribe to InforMed, and our next video gives you a five-part checklist to keep your muscle while the weight comes off.

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate, well hedged and safe. I checked the main claims against the sources, and they match:
- **Penn/BMJ study (BMJ press release):** sample sizes 12,004 vs 15,221 and 11,964 vs 11,233; hazard ratios 1.37 and 1.68; incidence 6.91 vs 5.04 per 1,000 person-years; authors call the absolute risk low; the extra risk was nonscarring; severity and regrowth weren't assessed; unmeasured confounding can't be ruled out; published July 22, 2026, which fits "this summer".
- **NYU Mendelian randomization study:** published in JID on Sept 3, 2026; 205,327 men; about 7% higher odds in genetically predisposed men; nobody in the study took the drug.
- **AJCD 2026 review:** points to rapid weight loss or related nutritional deficiencies as likely contributors to telogen effluvium.
- **AAD shedding page:** 50–100 hairs a day is normal; "Lost 20 pounds or more" is listed as a trigger; hair regains fullness within 6–9 months.
- **FDA:** biotin can cause falsely low troponin results.

Relative vs absolute risk is handled well, the limitations are stated, and the "talk to your prescriber" and "don't stop medication" lines are present. There are four minor issues, each with an exact fix:
1. The scarring-hair-loss sign cites a page that only covers one condition (CCCA), and the page doesn't mention redness.
2. The biotin "falsely high or falsely low" wording comes from a different FDA document than the one cited.
3. The advisory visual puts a paraphrase in quotation marks.
4. I couldn't open the PubMed URL for the BMJ paper (CAPTCHA), so it's unconfirmed.

Optional safety improvement: the FDA says biotin also interferes with thyroid (TSH, T4, T3) and ferritin tests. Those are the same tests the video suggests asking about, so s57 is a good place to connect them.

issues.claim: If the skin where hair has gone looks red, scaly, bumpy or shiny, especially with burning, itching or pain, that can signal scarring hair loss
issues.problem: The cited source (aad_scarring) is the AAD page for CCCA, which is one specific type of scarring hair loss, not scarring hair loss in general. It lists a scaly, bumpy or crusty scalp, a shiny and smooth scalp, and itching, pain, tenderness, burning or stinging. It does not mention redness. The narration generalizes from the source and adds 'red'.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "Sign three: scalp changes. If the skin where hair has gone looks scaly, bumpy or shiny, especially with burning, itching or pain, that can be a sign of scarring hair loss, which dermatologists want to see early." Keep aad_scarring as the source.

issues.claim: The FDA has warned that biotin ... can interfere with some lab tests and cause falsely high or falsely low results.
issues.problem: The cited FDA troponin page only confirms falsely LOW troponin results. The 'falsely high or falsely low' wording is in FDA's biotin interference guidance document, which isn't in the source list.
issues.fix: Add this source: {"id":"fda_biotin_guidance","title":"Testing for Biotin Interference in In Vitro Diagnostic Devices","publisher":"U.S. Food and Drug Administration","year":"2019","url":"https://www.fda.gov/media/127915/download"}. Then set the s55 source_ids to ["fda_biotin","fda_biotin_guidance"].

issues.claim: So if you take biotin or any supplement, tell your doctor before blood work.
issues.problem: This isn't an error, just a missed safety link. According to FDA, biotin can interfere with thyroid (TSH, T4, T3) and ferritin tests, which are the tests s50 suggests asking about. Viewers taking hair gummies could get misleading results from exactly those tests.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "So if you take biotin or any supplement, tell your doctor before blood work. FDA notes it can affect some thyroid and ferritin tests too, the very checks we just talked about." Set source_ids to ["fda_biotin","fda_biotin_guidance"].

issues.claim: Quote: "Protein is a priority during GLP-1 therapy, especially to help protect muscle."
issues.problem: A paraphrase is shown in quotation marks. The '(paraphrased)' tag helps, but the quote marks still suggest verbatim wording.
issues.fix: Change the visual kind from "quote" to "stat" or "broll", with on-screen text "Experts: prioritize protein to help protect muscle" and label "Joint advisory: ACLM, ASN, OMA, TOS (2025)". Or keep the quote layout and remove the quotation marks.

issues.problem: I couldn't confirm the PubMed page (CAPTCHA wall). The study itself, its title and its figures are confirmed by the BMJ Group press release.
issues.fix: Before publishing, check that PMID 42486607 resolves to this BMJ paper. Otherwise, replace the URL with the paper's bmj.com DOI link. The bmj_press source is enough to support every claim that cites bmj_penn.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are clean single-focal-point designs with the InforMed mascot style, but #1 ('SHED, NOT GONE') best balances curiosity and reassurance while staying directly on-topic: the comb/heart mascots visually reference hair loss and recovery, the gray-to-green color and sad-to-happy face pairing telegraphs a positive payoff without giving away the mechanism, and the headline is large, high-contrast, and reads instantly at phone size with zero clutter. #0's calendar mascot is clever conceptually (timing of shedding) but has no visual tie to hair, so it risks feeling disconnected or gimmicky in the feed even though the text itself is perfectly legible. #2 has the strongest 'hard number' curiosity hook (1.37x) and correctly includes a qualifier line per brand rules, but that qualifier renders very small at phone/thumbnail size, hurting legibility and making it harder to parse in under a second — a recurring issue flagged in our QA notes about tiny text. Given legibility ties in the winners' favor and #1 edges out #0 on relevance and emotional pull while avoiding #2's tiny-text risk, #1 is the strongest choice.

issues.fix:
Add these captions.

Instagram/Facebook: "Noticing more hair in your brush a few months into a GLP-1? Timing is the clue. In semaglutide (Wegovy) trials, about 3% reported hair loss vs 1% on placebo. The pattern most often described is telogen effluvium: delayed, even shedding after fast weight loss. It's typically temporary, and hair often grows back. What helps: protein first at each meal, a sensible pace agreed with your prescriber, and asking about ferritin, vitamin D and thyroid checks. See a dermatologist if shedding lasts 6+ months, comes in patches, or comes with scalp changes or pain. Educational only, not medical advice. issues.claim: Ozempic & GLP-1 Hair Loss: How Common It Is & Why It Often Grows Back
issues.problem: Brand names are allowed for recognition. But the trial figure in the video comes from Wegovy, and the cohort study covered GLP-1 diabetes drugs as a class. Putting 'Ozempic' first ties the findings to one product. This is wording polish, not a false claim.
issues.fix: Ozempic, Wegovy & GLP-1 Hair Loss: How Common It Is & Why It Often Grows Back

issues.problem: The script says 'typically temporary' and also flags three warning signs where shedding is not the usual kind. 'Usually' is close enough, but matching the script's wording keeps the packaging aligned with it.
